highlights.title: King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics
highlights.summary: The King spoke of "threats to our international order" in a letter marking the 10th anniversary of the National Cyber Security Centre.
body: King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.
Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

highlights.title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
highlights.summary: At this year's OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company's new AI agent Dots - and told the crowd that the company wants to "set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI." OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta's Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users'…
body: Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.

Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”

highlights.title: WandaVision Creator Set To Develop New Stargate Series
highlights.summary: After a failed attempt, Amazon MGM Studios is once again developing a Stargate series. According to Variety, the company is bringing on Jac Schaeffer, the showrunner of one of Disney Plus's most successful shows, WandaVision.
body: Amazon has wanted to create a Stargate TV series for a while now. Martin Gero, creator of Blindspot, had worked on various Stargate television series early in his career, so bringing him on board for a new series felt like the right move in 2025. Unfortunately, the project was canceled early in development.

According to Variety, Amazon was "concerned that Gero's take on the series would not have broad appeal." Despite these setbacks, Amazon wasn't ready to give up and was still on the prowl for a writer, and it seems it might've just found her.

Earlier this year, the company made a three-year deal with Jac Schaeffer. It is now taking advantage of the deal by handing her the Stargate project. You likely know Schaeffer best for her work as the creator of WandaVision and Agatha All Along, two critically acclaimed shows that reached the top of the charts on Disney Plus. Clearly, Amazon is hoping she can replicate that success with a Stargate show.

Very little is known about this project or how it differs from what Gero's take would've been. Regardless, Schaeffer will surely put her spin on the project and make it the best she possibly can for today's viewership.

highlights.title: ‘Rio,’ ‘Ice Age’ Director Carlos Saldanha on ‘Wonderful Homecoming’ With Ambitious Brazilian Adventure Film ‘100 Days’: ‘It Deserved a Big Cinema Treatment’
highlights.summary: It might have taken pioneering explorer Amyr Klink one hundred days to cross the Atlantic, but it took Carlos Saldanha almost three thousand to bring his story to the big screen.
body: Once he boarded the project, Saldanha reworked the script alongside Elena Soarez and Thais Tavares. The pandemic years slowed the project’s development, but granted the creative team more time to finesse the details of the adaptation. “To me, it wasn’t enough to just tell the tale of this hundred-day adventure,” says the director. “I was very interested in what was going on in Amyr’s head, what he did while he spent such a long time rowing all by himself, all alone in the sea.”

“I talked a lot with Amyr, with his family and friends, and did very in-depth research to understand who this person was and what moved him,” he adds. “Amyr was great in how much freedom he granted us. He helped us decipher him without having to spell it out for us.”

highlights.title: K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
highlights.summary: Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single " Nobody " was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.
body: Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.

In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.

Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “ Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.

My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.

highlights.title: Avatar: Seven Havens is a brilliant take-down of Korra's biggest haters
highlights.summary: The Korra series finale — as later seen in high-definition under normal connection speeds — is still one of my favorite endings (and favorite TV shows) of all time. But it’s hard to ignore the flaws; from a slashed budget that forced the animators to rely on still images for some pivotal scenes…
body: At the stroke of midnight on Dec. 19, 2014, Nickelodeon unceremoniously dumped the final two episodes of Avatar: The Legend of Korra on Nick.com. That night, I gathered on the couch with my roommate to witness the culmination of an epic four-season story. Unfortunately, 2014 streaming technology still had a long ways to go, and after watching Nickelodeon's online video player buffer for about 15 minutes, I gave up and went to bed. It was Thursday night, and I had work in the morning.

Seven Havens takes place over 200 years after Legend of Korra. A mysterious calamity has undone the industrial revolution that escalated across the previous two shows. Instead of the gleaming, utopian Republic City in Korra, or even the sprawling, walled kingdom of Ba Sing Se in The Last Airbender, there are seven fortified "havens" spread across this world, with seemingly nothing but inhospitable desert in between. Some time after the Four Nations invented hoverbikes, everything collapsed.

highlights.title: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
highlights.summary: After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed " unintended model actions," including submitting a false tip regarding an unsolved murder, that led…
body: Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.

The ability to gain access to the live internet, even when models were supposed to be operating in isolation, has been an ongoing issue for AI companies. Many incidents, including the Hugging Face attack, involved agents that were supposed to be denied access to the internet. Yet, in case after case, the agents found creative solutions to bypass those restrictions. Physically removing internet access would certainly improve security around AI testing, but it would also limit its usefulness.

highlights.title: Alphonse Le Grande edges Sea Lantern for historic Cesarewitch win
highlights.summary: Alphonse Le Grande became only the second horse in history to win the Club Godolphin Cesarewitch twice when coming with a late rattle to foil a major gamble on Sea Lantern at Newmarket.
body: The Tony Martin-trained seven-year-old stayed on strongly under 5lb claimer Patrick McGettigan to cut down 4-1 favourite Sea Lantern who had hit the front with less than a furlong to run, with the winner landing the historic handicap by a short head. The well-backed Dawn Rising, runner-up 12 months ago, was third, with High Fibre fourth.
The victory repeated Alphonse Le Grande's 2024 win, seeing him emulate Aaim To Prosper who won the race in 2010 and 2012.

Martin - who was serving a three-month suspension which meant Cathy O'Leary held the licence when Alphonse Le Grande struck two years ago - said: "I couldn't believe it, I thought we had ruined our chances by running two weeks ago at the Curragh. But he's such a tough little horse he pulled it out the bag. He keeps turning up when we need him and on better ground he finds another gear.
"I didn't know we had got it, but I'm delighted he got the right result in the photo - I just need to make sure the jockey weighs in!

highlights.title: I Have Discovered The Best Game Soundtrack of 2026 and It Is Super Woden: Rally Edge
highlights.summary: Video game soundtracks are pretty respectable these days. Earlier this year, I watched James Bond composer David Arnold take the stage at the BAFTA Games Awards and pay tribute to the medium before presenting an award to Toma Otowa for the Ghost of Yōtei soundtrack.
body: It's mostly high-energy stuff, as befits a game about sending toylike cars hurtling and powersliding along two-minute rally stages. It's also quite retro, as befits a game with a kind of cel-shaded PS1 aesthetic. It consists of EDM, metal, hip-hop, and jazz-funk rendered with a synthetic MIDI sound that pairs naturally with vibrant low-poly graphics and blocky, functional menus.

It's a soundtrack of two halves, provided by two different artists. DJ DeVito provides the spine: a suite of techno, Eurodance, electro, and happy hardcore, all of it relentlessly and joyously upbeat. "Drive or Die" is infectiously jolly, powered by an insistent bassline and amusingly 80s synthesized orchestra stabs. "Across the Universe" is another example of DJ DeVito's hilariously insistent four-to-the-floor techno.
A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

This solid foundation is then built on by the work of a true wizard called DonutDroid who puts the Super Woden: Rally Edge soundtrack on a whole new level. DonutDroid's ability to flit between musical genres while maintaining a consistent sound and vibe is truly amazing.

highlights.summary: Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.
body: Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.

There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks.
Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of the Channels podcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back to Decoder.

In a statement released on Friday, the PPD said the AI model sent the tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18th, but the…
body: The false tip ‘purported to come from someone who might have information about the case.’

Anthropic learned its AI model sent the false tip on September 28th and notified the PPD on October 7th. The company said that during testing, its AI model was interacting with “randomly selected websites” and submitted false information through the PPD’s tipline, according to the PPD’s statement. The submission “purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.

After discovering the submission, Anthropic halted the testing process that led to the false tip. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google have been the subject of increased scrutiny after disclosing that their AI models escaped testing environments and hacked third-party companies. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, advocated for slowing down the development of AI in response to these incidents.
Anthropic also notes in its report that “Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”

highlights.title: AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals
highlights.summary: Anti-cybercrime initiatives are increasingly using AI to scam the scammers by tricking them into talking to lifelike bots that they think are real victims.
body: Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.

For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.
points: Anti-cybercrime initiatives are increasingly using AI to scam the scammers by tricking them into talking to lifelike bots that they think are real victims.

highlights.title: Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting
highlights.summary: Workers at three major publishing houses tell WIRED that LLMs are being used for publicity, cover art, back cover copy, and emails, as some execs push junior staff to champion the tech.
body: In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.

According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.

At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body —are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.

Three weeks have passed since the massive Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and only two weeks are left until Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. Time for the hands-on previews, then, and Polygon's Mike McWhertor duly reports that Switch Sports Resort is a perfectly chill compilation that channels WaveRace, Pilotwings, and even Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, as well as the mighty Wii Sports.

We all know this is just the build-up, though. Just two weeks after Switch Sports Resort comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a remake so consequential, of a game so revered, that it effectively has the status of a brand-new mainline Zelda game. I've heard a plausible but unverified rumor that this is how it's being treated internally; that, rather than entrust the remake to an outside developer like Grezzo (which handled Ocarina of Time 3D and the Link's Awakening remake), Nintendo made it in-house.

Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west…
body: Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.
When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere.

Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople.

Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16.

highlights.title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
highlights.summary: For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once.
body: In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.

Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.

body: The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”

Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison.
